summary:
The Northwest Territories is a territory of Canada. Criminal law, human rights protections and entry rules are set nationally rather than by the territory, and the territory's own legislative activity on transgender issues concerns vital statistics and name change.

In June 2026 the Legislative Assembly was taking feedback from police and from the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act intended to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people. The proposals include an option for trans and non-binary people to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. This is the first on-record territorial legislation in the Northwest Territories specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people. The amendments were under consultation and had not been enacted.

The RCMP has taken a position against part of the proposal. Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith asked MLAs to remove or amend the registrar general's option not to notify authorities, arguing that criminal records are tied to a person's legal name and that officers may put themselves in danger if records are not transferred to a new name. Yellowknife North MLA Shauna Morgan pressed the RCMP on how officers would verify legal names without identification. The police service is therefore on record opposing a measure designed to keep a trans person's former name out of public view.

Organised community support for trans and Two-Spirit young people is documented in the territory. In June 2023 the Beaufort Delta Education Council bused seventeen regional students into Inuvik for pride events centred on feeling comfortable in one's own gender and sexuality, with workshops led by Two-Spirit Anishinaabe/Metis musician G.R. Gritt, a screening of 'Small Town Pride' and a pride parade. The gathering included a moment of silence at the Inuvik Community Greenhouse for Frank Gruben, an LGBTQ2S community member from Aklavik missing since 2023.

Tulita, a small hamlet on the Mackenzie River in the Sahtu region, held its first Pride celebration on 28 June 2025, organised jointly by Chief Albert Wright School, the hamlet administration and the local RCMP detachment. Const. Matt Ryan counted more than 50 attendees and described the day as creating a safe and welcoming space for the 2SLGBTQI+ community. The RCMP covered food and paint while the hamlet and school supplied volunteers, firewood and the venue.
tangentialFactors:
The RCMP's position at the Legislative Assembly and the Tulita detachment's role in the 2025 Pride celebration are both on the record, and they run in opposite directions. The force argued at the legislature against a measure that would keep a trans person's former name out of the gazette and away from automatic notification, while a detachment in the Sahtu region helped fund and staff a Pride event whose officer described the day as welcoming the 2SLGBTQI+ community.

The two documented community events are separated by two years and by geography: a regional centre gathering in Inuvik in 2023 that drew students from across the Beaufort Delta, and a first-ever hamlet Pride in Tulita in 2025. Both were organised with public institutions, the education council in the first case and the school, hamlet administration and RCMP detachment in the second.
localsOnly:
A name change in the Northwest Territories is published in the NWT Gazette, and the registrar general holds an option to notify authorities. Both provisions are the subject of the current review, so a resident who needs a name change kept out of public view is relying on an amendment that has not been enacted.

In Tulita, organisers planned monthly inclusive school events from September 2025, run through the school and the hamlet administration with the local RCMP detachment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act were still under consultation in June 2026. Whether the registrar general's option not to notify authorities survives, and whether the gazette non-publication option is enacted, is unresolved.

No territorial breakdown of national hate-crime statistics is published, and reporting infrastructure in the territories is thin relative to metropolitan areas, so no Northwest Territories rate can be derived from the national series. Egale Canada's national analysis of police-reported hate-crime data contains no territorial data.

Frank Gruben's disappearance from Aklavik in 2023 remains unresolved. No anti-trans motive has been documented, and the case is not evidence of trans-specific targeting in the territory.
